## Overview

I'm a hardware and firmware researcher in the
[Analog Circuit Lab](https://www.hmc.edu/engineering/undergraduate-research-experiences/matthew-spencer-research-group/)
at Harvey Mudd, working on instrumentation for the USDA. The lab builds
[electropenetrographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_penetration_graph) (EPGs): instruments that wire a
live insect and its host plant into a circuit to record the tiny electrical signals produced as the insect feeds.
Agricultural researchers use these recordings to study the feeding behavior of disease-vector insects.

My work spans the whole signal chain: the low-noise analog front end that picks up the signal, the power system
that runs it in the field, and the firmware that configures the board and streams data to a computer.

## Analog Front End

- Designed low-noise analog front ends with impedance matching, instrumentation amplifiers, and up to **7,000x gain**
  to resolve the small signals produced during insect feeding.
- Moved a dual-battery instrument to a **single-supply design with integrated battery management**, simplifying
  field deployment.
- Prototyped and tuned circuits on the bench with oscilloscopes, function generators, and power supplies to improve
  signal quality and reliability.

The current electropenetrograph board pairs a DDS-based signal-generation chain with a synchronized acquisition
chain. Onboard control logic sets gain, switching, and calibration on the fly through analog and digital multiplexers,
a DAC output stage, and digitally controlled rheostats, with onboard battery charger and monitor ICs.

## Firmware

- Developed **nRF5340** firmware on the **Zephyr RTOS**, with SPI, I&sup2;C, and ADC drivers that configure gain,
  offset, and excitation on the analog board.
- Wrote **Bluetooth** firmware that streams measurements to client software in real time.
- Built Python tools to acquire, process, and visualize recordings from feeding experiments.
